title: Chromosome numbers of germ-nuclei mostly lie between six and sixteen

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Chromosome numbers of germ-nuclei mostly lie between six and sixteen

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Although chromosome number is constant within a species, the range of numbers across plants and animals is small: few organisms have fewer than six chromosomes in the germ-nuclei and fewer still have more than sixteen.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: (as regards the germ-nuclei) few organisms have less than six chromosomes, and fewer still have more than sixteen

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IV, “On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell”; topic “Biological significance of mitotic figures”. Scope: germ-nuclei (haploid chromosome number) of plants and animals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch04-13: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.90

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The numerical bounds and target distribution are explicit and readily refutable. Large public chromosome and genome databases provide broad enough coverage for a modern assessment, though bias correction is needed.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compile haploid chromosome numbers across documented plant and animal species and calculate the fractions below six, from six through sixteen, and above sixteen, with taxonomic and sampling corrections. The claim is supported only if the tails are genuinely rare across both kingdoms.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Counts are taxonomically and publication biased.

Ploidy and haploid-versus-diploid notation require harmonization.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.98
data existence: 0.9
discriminating power: 0.98
analysis feasibility: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is a frequency statement about germ-nucleus chromosome number, and both plants and animals now have open count compilations large enough to estimate the two tails. The analysis is a histogram. Uneven taxonomy and diploid reporting reduce adequacy below a complete census, but they do not prevent a clear decision about whether counts are mostly confined to six through sixteen.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Using haploid counts for plant and animal species, compute the fraction with fewer than six chromosomes and the fraction with more than sixteen. The claim stands if both tails are small and the upper tail is the smaller; it falls if a large share of species lie outside 6–16, especially above 16.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
B chromosomes and sex chromosomes create within-species ranges.

Animal sampling is uneven across phyla.

Plant records are often sporophytic diploid numbers, so haploid values need a ploidy assumption.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Across plant and animal species, the gametic (haploid) chromosome number n lies mostly between 6 and 16: the fraction of taxa with n < 6 is small and the fraction with n > 16 is smaller still.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Fetched the CCDB statistics CSV for each of the four plant major groups (69,948 species rows; median parsed n per species) and parsed the ACC data table embedded in its download page (12,221 animal records; haploid N where given, else 2N/2). Collapsed to one median value per species and per genus, then computed the fractions of taxa with n < 6, 6 <= n <= 16 and n > 16 for plants and animals at both resolutions, plus breakdowns by plant major group and animal phylum and a histogram (derived/histograms.csv).

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Plants: species-level gametic numbers from the Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB) statistics service for all four major groups (Angiosperms, Gymnosperms, Pteridophytes, Bryophytes), using each species' median parsed n. Animals: the Animal Chromosome Count Database (ACC) table (haploid N where given, else 2N/2), one median value per species. For each kingdom compute f_low = fraction of taxa with n < 6, f_mid = fraction with 6 <= n <= 16, f_high = fraction with n > 16, at two resolutions: species level, and genus level (median of species values per genus, the primary resolution, to damp sampling bias toward well-studied genera). Supports if at genus level, in both kingdoms, f_low <= 0.10 and f_high <= 0.10 and f_high <= f_low.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Refutes if at genus level f_high >= 0.25 in either kingdom (more than a quarter of genera above 16 is not 'fewer still'), or if f_high > f_low in both kingdoms (the upper tail is the larger tail, inverting the claim). Mixed otherwise (e.g. one kingdom satisfies the bounds and the other does not, without reaching the refutation thresholds).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of animal genera with haploid n > 16 (plant genera: 0.320); fraction with n < 6: animals 0.080, plants 0.011

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: database census; genus-level n = 8414 plant and 5285 animal genera, species-level n = 64926 and 12221

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Thompson's 'germ-nuclei' chromosome number is the gametic number n (half the somatic 2n), which both databases provide or allow (CCDB parses counts to gametophytic n; ACC lists N or 2N). 'Few' and 'fewer still' are read as tail fractions of at most 10%, with the upper tail no larger than the lower. The claim is about organisms generally, so species (or genera) are the units, each counted once, with no phylogenetic weighting; the species-level figures are reported alongside the primary genus-level ones. Databases are biased toward studied taxa (crops, insects, vertebrates), which is noted but not corrected beyond the genus-level aggregation.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB), species-level statistics for Angiosperms, Gymnosperms, Pteridophytes, Bryophytes

Animal Chromosome Count Database (ACC; Roman-Palacios et al. 2021), table embedded in the download page

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The lower bound holds (only 1.1% of plant genera and 8.0% of animal genera have n < 6) and the modal haploid number (9-13) sits inside Thompson's 6-16 window, so the claim is half right; what fails is the upper bound: 32% of plant genera and 41% of animal genera have n > 16, so the upper tail is roughly 30 and 5 times larger than the lower tail, the reverse of 'fewer still'.

Both databases over-represent studied taxa (crops, insects, vertebrates) and plants are counted as gametophytic numbers including polyploids (hexaploid wheat is n = 21). Even taking the most favourable subsets (gymnosperms 5.8% > 16; bryophytes 11%), ferns (96% > 16), vertebrates (74%) and molluscs (60%) leave the general claim refuted.

ACC records with non-numeric or range entries for 2N and N were dropped; odd 2N values (XO systems) give half-integer n, which does not affect the 6-16 binning.

Thompson wrote in 1917 from a handful of counted species; the finding reflects a century of counting rather than an error in his reading of the data available to him.
